Antonio Vivaldi. An Italian Baroque composer and virtuoso violinist born in 1678 and died in 1741 who profoundly shaped the development of the concerto form and instrumental music. His energetic, rhythmically driving compositions, extraordinary technical demands for the violin, and prolific output of nearly 500 works, including over 200 violin concertos, made him one of the most influential composers of the Baroque era. His music influenced contemporaries including Bach and later shaped the Classical symphony.

Vivaldi was born in Venice into a musical family and studied violin from childhood, developing into one of the era's most accomplished virtuoso performers. He served as master of the Ospedale's ensemble, an orphanage and conservatory in Venice, where he wrote and premiered many of his concertos for talented young musicians. He mastered and standardized the concerto form, particularly the ritornello structure, which alternates between full ensemble and solo episodes. This created a template that Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven would adopt for generations to come.

His most famous work is The Four Seasons, a set of four violin concertos depicting spring, summer, autumn, and winter through vivid musical imagery. It remains one of the world's most performed compositions. His compositions feature rapid, driving rhythms, bright orchestration, and virtuosic solo passages, establishing the exciting, entertainment-focused aesthetic that distinguished Baroque instrumental music. Though he also composed operas, his instrumental works achieved greater lasting fame and influence. His technique of rapid figuration, sudden dynamic contrasts, and clear harmonic structures made his music immediately appealing and widely copied, with his influence on orchestral writing lasting well into the nineteenth century, connecting him to the broader traditions of Baroque music, the concerto form, and the violin itself.
